The fourth: al-Haqqah is in the sense of al-Haqqah (a more specific and binding form of haqq), and al-Haqqah is more specific than al-Haqq and more binding. The fifth: al-Layth said: al-Haqqah is the calamity that has come upon the one who is afflicted by it, so there is no falsehood in it; and this is the meaning of His, exalted is He, saying: ﴿There is no denying its occurrence﴾ (al-Waqi'ah: 2).

The sixth: al-Haqqah is the Hour in which the recompense for every error and guidance becomes due, and it is the Resurrection.

The seventh: al-Haqqah is the time that becomes due for the people to befall them.

The eighth: it is the Truth in that all the effects of the actions of the responsible persons will be in it, for on that day reward and punishment take place, and it goes beyond the limit of waiting. This is the saying of al-Zajjaj.

The original form would be "al-Haqqah ma hiya," i.e., "what is it?", to exalt its matter and magnify its terror. The apparent noun was placed in the position of the pronoun because it is more frightening for it. A similar example is His saying: ﴿al-Qari'ah﴾ ﴿ma al-Qari'ah﴾

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 69, verses 4–6:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Thamud and 'Ad denied the Striking Calamity.﴾

﴿The Striking Calamity⁠﴾ is that which strikes people with terrors and dreadful events, the heaven with splitting and cleaving, the earth and the mountains with pounding and scattering, and the stars with being obliterated and dispersed. He said ﴿denied the Striking Calamity⁠﴾ and did not say "denied it" in order to indicate that the meaning of striking is present in the Inevitable Reality (al-Haqqah), so that this is an addition to the description of its severity. When He mentioned it and magnified it, He followed that with mention of those who denied it and what befell them because of their denial, as a reminder to the people of Makkah and a warning to them of the consequences of their denial.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿As for Thamud, they were destroyed by the Overwhelming Blast.⁠﴾

Know that there are several views concerning al-Taghiyah (the overwhelming, transgressing thing):

The first: al-Taghiyah is the event that exceeds the limit in intensity and force. He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿When the water overflowed⁠﴾ (al-Haqqah: 11), meaning it exceeded its limit, and He said: ﴿The gaze did not swerve, nor did it transgress⁠﴾ (al-Najm: 17). According to this view, al-Taghiyah is a suppressed qualifier (na't mahdhuf, an omitted adjective), and they differed about that omitted word. Some of them said it is the Cry that exceeds other cries in force and intensity. He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿Indeed, We sent upon them a single Cry, and they became like the dry remnants of a fence-builder's enclosure⁠﴾ (al-Qamar: 31). Others said it is the quake (al-Rajfah), and others said it is the thunderbolt (al-Sa'iqah).

The second view: al-Taghiyah here means transgression (al-tughyan), so it is a verbal noun (masdar), like al-Kadhibah, al-Baqiyah, al-'Aqibah and al-'Afiyah. That is, they were destroyed by their transgression against God, since they denied His messengers and disbelieved in Him. This is reported from Ibn 'Abbas. Later scholars criticized it from two angles:

The first, which al-Zajjaj said: when He mentioned in the second clause the kind of thing with which the punishment came, which is His saying ﴿with a furious wind⁠﴾, it is necessary that the situation in the first clause be likewise, so that the correspondence is present.

The second, which al-Qadi said: if what was meant were what they said, then the proper wording would have been "they were destroyed by it and because of it" (uhlikū lahā wa li-ajlihā).

The third view: ﴿by al-Taghiyah⁠﴾ means by the group among Thamud who transgressed, so they conspired to hamstring the she-camel and hamstrung her. That is, they were destroyed by the evil of their transgressing group. It is also possible that al-Taghiyah means that single man who undertook to hamstring the she-camel and destroyed everyone, since they approved of his deed; so he was called "al-Taghiyah," just as one says: so-and-so is "rawiyat al-shi'r" (a great transmitter of poetry), "dahiyah" (a shrewd, cunning person), "'allamah" (a great scholar), and "nassabah" (an expert genealogist).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿As for 'Ad, they were destroyed by a furious, roaring wind⁠﴾. Al-Sarsar is the one that is very loud in its sound, having a sarsarah (roar). It was also said: it is the cold one, from al-sirr (intense cold), as if it were one in which cold was repeated and multiplied, so that it burns with the intensity of its cold. As for al-'Atiyah (the violent, overpowering one), there are views concerning it:

The first: al-Kalbi said: it rebelled against its guardians that day, so they did not keep account of how much of it went out. Nothing of it came out before that or after that except in a known measure. He, upon him be prayers and peace, said: "The water transgressed against its keepers on the day of Noah, and the wind rebelled against its keepers on the day of 'Ad, so it had no way over them." According to this view, it is "rebellious against the keepers."

The second: 'Ata reported from Ibn 'Abbas: he means the wind rebelled against 'Ad, so they could not repel it by any stratagem, whether by hiding behind a building or leaning on a mountain, for it used to tear them from their hiding places and destroy them.

The third view: this is not the rebellion (al-'utuww) that is disobedience. Rather, it means reaching a thing and its end. From it comes their saying: "al-nabt 'ata" (the plant reached its limit and dried out). He, may He be exalted, said: ﴿And I have indeed reached extreme old age⁠﴾ (Maryam: 8). So "'atiyah" means reaching its limit in strength and intensity.

Commentary of al-Razi (*Mafatih al-Ghayb*) on surah 69, verses 7–9:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿He subjected it against them for seven nights and eight days, in succession﴾. Muqatil said: "He let it loose upon them." Al-Zajjaj said: "He uprooted it against them." Others said: "He sent it against them." These are the expressions transmitted from the exegetes. In my view there is a subtle point here. Some people say that those winds grew violent only because a planetary conjunction of the stars required it. So His saying ﴿subjected it﴾ indicates the rejection of that doctrine and clarifies that this occurred only by God's decree and power. Had it not been for this precise point, the warning and the admonition against punishment would not have been conveyed.

As for His saying ﴿seven nights and eight days, in succession﴾, its benefit is that if He had not mentioned it, the duration of this punishment would not have been known. When He said ﴿seven nights and eight days﴾, the length of this time became known. Then, since someone might suppose that the punishment was scattered over this period, He removed that supposition by His saying ﴿ḥusūman﴾, meaning continuous and consecutive. The scholars differed about ḥusūman (uninterrupted, from ḥasm, to cut off completely) in several ways:

The first, which is the view of most, is that ḥusūman means "in succession," i.e., these days followed one another upon them with the destructive wind, so there was no slackening or interruption in them. According to this view, ḥusūm is the plural of ḥāsim (one who cuts off), like shuhūd and quʿūd. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 69, verses 13–14:

He said: ﴿Then when the Trumpet is blown with a single blast﴾, and in this there are several issues:

The first issue: ﴿nafkhah﴾ (blast) has been read with both nominative (raf') and accusative (nasb). The reading with the nominative is that the verb is attributed to it (i.e., it is the subject), and the masculine form of the verb is acceptable because of the separation (al-fasl). The reading with the accusative is that the verb is attributed to the prepositional phrase (al-jarr wa al-majrur), and then ﴿nafkhah﴾ is put in the accusative as a verbal noun (masdar).

The second issue: The single blast intended here is the first blast, because at it the destruction of the world occurs. If it is said: why did He say after that, ﴿On that Day you will be presented﴾, while the presentation (al-'ard) occurs at the second blast? We say: He made "the Day" a name for the extended period in which the two blasts occur, the swoon (al-sa'qah) and the resurrection (al-nushur), and the standing and the reckoning. Therefore He said ﴿On that Day you will be presented﴾, just as you say: "I came to him in the year such-and-such," though your coming was in one particular time of that period.

[Issue] 4: The anthropomorphists (al-Mushabbihah) said: if God were not in the Throne, then carrying the Throne would be pointless and without benefit, especially since this is confirmed by His saying, exalted is He: ﴿On that Day you will be presented﴾ [al-Haqqah 69:18], and the presentation only takes place if God were located in the Throne. So we know that it necessarily requires interpretation. We say: the reason for this statement is that He, exalted is He, addressed them in terms of what they are accustomed to. Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 69, verses 18–19:

His saying, Most High: ﴿On that Day you will be exposed (to judgment)﴾. Al-ʿarḍ (exposure) is an expression for reckoning and questioning. It is likened to a sultan reviewing his troops in order to learn their condition. Its parallel is His saying: ﴿And they will be presented before your Lord in rows﴾ [al-Kahf: 48]. It is narrated: "On the Day of Resurrection there are three exposures. As for two of them, they involve excuse-making, argument, and rebuke. As for the third, the books will be scattered, and the blessed one will take his book in his right hand, and the doomed one his book in his left hand."

﴿Not a thing concealed of you will be hidden﴾. ﴿As for him who is given his record in his right hand﴾ ﴿he will say, "Here, read my record!"﴾.

* * *

Then He said: ﴿Not a thing concealed of you will be hidden﴾. Concerning it there are two issues.

The first issue: there are two interpretations of the verse.

The first: the explanation of the verse is that "you will be exposed, and your affair will not be hidden, for He knows everything, and not a thing concealed of you is hidden from Him." Its parallel is His saying: ﴿Nothing of them is hidden from Allah﴾ [Ghafir: 16]. Thus the purpose is to intensify the threat, meaning: you will be exposed before One for whom nothing is hidden at all.

The second interpretation: the meaning is that on the Day of Resurrection there will be disclosed what was hidden of you in this world, for the states of the believers will become manifest, so their joy is completed thereby, and the states of the people of punishment will become manifest, so their grief and disgrace become evident thereby. This is what is meant by His saying: ﴿On the Day when secrets are tested﴾ ﴿then he will have no power nor any helper﴾ [al-Tariq: 9]. In this there is the greatest restraint and warning, which is the fear of disgrace.

The second issue: the reading of the majority is "lā takhfā" with a ta' dotted from above. Abu ʿUbayda preferred the yāʾ, which is the reading of Hamza and al-Kisaʾi. He said: "Because the yāʾ is permissible for both masculine and feminine, whereas the tāʾ is permissible only for the feminine. Here, attributing the verb to the masculine is permissible, namely if the intended meaning of al-khafiya is a thing that has concealment." Moreover, a separation has occurred here between the noun and the verb by His saying: "of you" (minkum).

Know that when He, Most High, mentioned where this exposure ends, He said: ﴿As for him who is given his record in his right hand, he will say, "Here, read my record!"﴾ Concerning it there are two issues.

The first issue: hāʾ (here) is an interjection uttered with a sound, from which is understood the meaning of "take," like "uff" and "ḥass." Abu al-Qasim al-Zajjaji said: "There are dialects of it, and the best of them is what Sibawayh related from the Arabs, when he said: Among what is commanded from the explicit forms are their saying: hāʾ, yā fatā (here, O youth), meaning take hold, and they pronounce the hamza with a fatha and make its fatha a marker of the masculine, just as they say: hāk, yā fatā, so the fatha of the kāf is made a sign of the masculine." It is said to two persons: hāʾumā, and to a group: hāʾumū and hāʾum. The mīm in this position is like the mīm in antumā and antum. This ḍamma that arose on the hamza of hāʾum is in fact the ḍamma of the mīm of the plural, because the original form is hāʾumū and antumū, so they prolonged the ḍamma and gave the dual the ruling of the plural, since the dual is in their view treated like the plural in many rulings.

The second issue: when two governing words act upon one governed word, the governing of the nearer one is permissible by consensus. As for the governing of the farther one, is it permissible or not? The Kufans held it to be permissible, while the Basrans prohibited it. The Basrans argued for their view with this verse, because His saying ﴿hāʾum﴾ is governing, and His saying ﴿iqraʾū﴾ is also governing. So if the governing word were the farther one, the construction would be: "hāʾum kitābiyah," and it would be required to say: "iqraʾūhu." A parallel is: (﴿Bring me, I will pour over it molten copper﴾ [al-Kahf: 96]). Know that this argument is weak, because this verse indicates that what occurs here is the governing of the nearer one, and that is not disputed. The dispute is only whether the governing of the farther one is permissible, and the verse contains no reference to that. Also, the pronoun may be omitted, because its clarity makes explicit mention unnecessary, as in His saying: ﴿And the men who remember Allah much and the women who remember﴾ [al-Ahzab: 35]. So why should it not be the case here as well? Then the Kufans argued that the first governing word is prior in existence to the second governing word, and the first governing word, when it came into existence, required a governed word, since the cause cannot occur without its effect. So the governed word becoming governed by the first governing word precedes the existence of the second governing word, and the second governing word came into existence only after it had become governed by the first governing word. Therefore it is impossible that it should also become governed by the second governing word, because a single ruling cannot be caused by two causes, and because what has already been caused cannot be caused by what comes afterward. This issue is one of the subtleties of grammar.

The third issue: the hāʾ is for pausing in "kitābiyah," and likewise in "ḥisābiyah, māliyah, and sulṭāniyah." The rule for these hāʾs is that they be present in pausing and dropped in continuous speech. Since these hāʾs are written in the Mushaf, and what is written in the Mushaf must be present in pronunciation, and their pronunciation was appropriate only at pausing, they therefore preferred pausing for this reason. Some were bold enough to drop these hāʾs in continuous speech, and Ibn Muhaysin recited with a sukūn on the yāʾ without them. A group recited with the hāʾ present both in continuous speech and in pausing, in adherence to the Mushaf.

The fourth issue: know that when he is given his record in his right hand, and then he says: ﴿Here, read my record!﴾, this indicates that he has reached the utmost of joy, because when he has been given his record in his right hand, he knows that he is among the saved and among those who are successful with bliss, so he loves to make that known to others so that they may rejoice in what he has attained. It is also said: he says this to the people of his household and his relatives.

Then He relates of him that he says: ﴿Indeed, I was certain that I would encounter my reckoning﴾.

The second: The implied sense is: "I used to think that I would encounter my reckoning, whereupon God would hold me to account for my misdeeds; but He graciously pardoned me and did not hold me to account for them. So ﴿Take, read my record﴾."

The third: Abu Hurayra narrated that he (ﷺ) said: "A man will be brought forth on the Day of Resurrection and his record will be given to him. His good deeds will appear on the back of his palm, and his bad deeds will be written on the inside of his palm. He will look at his bad deeds and grieve. It will be said to him, 'Turn over your palm,' and he will look at it and see his good deeds and rejoice. Then he will say: ﴿Take, read my record﴾ — ﴿Indeed, I was certain﴾ at the first glance — ﴿that I would encounter my reckoning﴾, in the sense of severity. But now God has relieved me of that distress." As for the wretched, it will be the opposite of what we have mentioned.

The fourth: "Ṭanantu" means "I knew" (ʿalimtu). It is treated as equivalent to knowledge because a predominant conjecture is given the status of knowledge in customary practice and in legal rulings. It is said: "I am certain (aẓunnu ẓannan ka-l-yaqin) that the matter is such and such."

The fifth: What is meant is: "I was certain in the world that, on account of the deeds I used to do in the world, I would reach these ranks in the Resurrection." Now I have attained certainty, so the word ẓann (conjecture) remains in its apparent sense, because the people of the world do not affirm such things with certainty.

Then God, exalted is He, explained the outcome of his affair, saying: ﴿So he will be in a pleasing life﴾. And here there are two issues:

The first issue: describing the life as "pleasing" (rāḍiyah) has two aspects:

The first: the meaning is that it is attributed to pleasing (riḍā), like "one wearing armour" (dāri') and "one bearing arrows" (nābil). The attribution (nisbah) is of two kinds: an attribution by particles (ḥurūf) and an attribution by form (ṣīghah).

The second: He made pleasing (riḍā) a property of the life metaphorically, even though its possessor is the one who lives it.

The second issue: The scholars stated in defining reward (thawāb) that it must be a benefit, it must be pure of impurities, it must be lasting, and it must be accompanied by honour. Thus the meaning is only "pleased with" from every aspect if it includes these attributes. So His saying ﴿a pleasing life﴾ is a word comprising all of these conditions that we have mentioned.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 69, verses 25–27:

God, exalted is He, says: ﴿But as for him who is given his record in his left hand, he will say: "Oh, I wish I had not been given my record, and had not known what my reckoning is!"﴾

Know that God, exalted is He, has made clear that when he looks into his record and recalls the ugliness of his deeds, he is overcome with shame at them, and the punishment resulting from that shame becomes greater than the punishment of the Fire. So he says: "Would that they had punished me with the Fire, and had not presented this record to me, which reminded me of the ugliness of my deeds, so that I would not fall into this shame." This alerts you to the fact that spiritual punishment is more severe than physical punishment. As for His words, ﴿and had not known what my reckoning is!﴾, meaning: "and I had not known what my reckoning is," because it is complete and there is no benefit to him in that reckoning; rather, all of it is against him.

* * *

Then He says: ﴿Oh, would that it had been the one that ended me!﴾ To what does the pronoun in "Oh would that it had" refer? There are two possibilities:

The first: it refers to the first death. Although it has not been mentioned, its obviousness makes it as if it had been mentioned. "Al-qadiyah" means the one that cuts off from life, and it carries an indication of finality and completion. God, exalted is He, says: ﴿Then when it is finished﴾ [al-Jumu'ah: 10], and it is said: "qudiya ʿala fulan," meaning he died. So the meaning is: "Would that the death I died had been the one that cut off my affair, so that I would not be resurrected after it, and would not meet what I have reached." Qatadah said: he wished for death, and there was nothing more hateful to him in the world than death; and worse than death is that for which death is sought. The poet said:

"And worse than death is that which, if you meet it, you wish for death from it, while death is greater."

The second: it refers to the state he witnessed upon studying the record. The meaning: "Would that this state had been the death that finished me off," because he saw that state as more horrifying and bitter than whatever he had tasted of the bitterness and severity of death, so he wished for death in its presence.

﴿What has availed﴾ is a negation and interrogation in the sense of denial, meaning: what thing has availed me the wealth that I possessed? A parallel to it is His saying: ﴿And they will come to Us individually﴾ [Maryam: 80]. The first: Ibn 'Abbas said: "My proof, with which I used to argue against Muhammad in the world, has gone astray from me." Muqatil said: "My proof has gone astray from me," meaning when the limbs testified against him to his polytheism.

The first: the purpose is not measurement by this exact quantity, but description as long, as in His saying: ﴿If you ask forgiveness for them seventy times﴾, meaning many times.

The second: it is measured by this quantity. Then they said: each cubit is seventy spans (bā'), and each span is farther than the distance between Makkah and Kufa. Al-Hasan said: "God knows best which cubit it is." His saying ﴿so insert him﴾: al-Mubarrad said: one says "salaka-hu" in the road, in the chain, and other things, and "aslaktuhu" means "I caused him to enter." Al-Kalbi said: just as a thread is passed through pearls, and then the rest of it is placed around his neck.

Know that when the Exalted explained this severe punishment, He mentioned its cause, saying:

﴿Indeed, he did not believe in Allah, the Mighty﴾ ﴿and did not urge the feeding of the needy.﴾

The first is an indication of the corruption of the state of the rational faculty (al-quwwah al-'aqilah), and the second is an indication of the corruption of the state of the practical faculty (al-quwwah al-'amaliyyah). Here there are several issues:

The first issue: As for His saying, ﴿and did not urge the feeding of the needy﴾, there are two opinions concerning it:

One of them: and he did not urge the giving of food to the needy.

The second: that "food" (ta'am) here is a noun placed in the position of the verbal noun (al-ital'am, "feeding"), just as "gift" (ata') is placed in the position of "giving" (i'ta') in the saying of the poet:

"And after your gift of a hundred camels in pasture..."

The second issue: The author of al-Kashshaf (al-Zamakhshari) said: As for His saying, ﴿and did not urge the feeding of the needy﴾, it contains two strong proofs of the great gravity of the offense of withholding from the needy:
One of them: He joined it to disbelief and made it a companion to it.

The second: He mentioned "urging" (al-hadd) rather than the act itself, so that it would be known that one who abandons urging is in this rank, so how about one who abandons the act itself?

The third issue: The verse indicates that disbelievers are punished for abandoning the prayer and the zakat, and this is what we mean when we say that they are addressed with the branches of the sacred law (furu' al-shara'i'). It is related from Abu al-Darda' that he used to urge his wife to make more broth for the sake of the needy, and he would say: "We have removed half of the chain by faith; shall we not remove the remaining half?" It was also said: the intended meaning is the prevention of disbelievers, and their saying: ﴿Shall we feed one whom, if Allah willed, He would feed?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 47].

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 69, verses 36–40:

The statement of the Exalted: ﴿Nor any food except from ghislin﴾. On this there are two issues.

The first issue: It is related that Ibn 'Abbas was asked about the *ghislin* (a discharge of pus and blood from the people of the Fire, a term that means the filth or pus of the damned), and he said: "I do not know what the *ghislin* is." Al-Kalbi said: it is a water that flows from the people of the Fire, of pus, discharge and blood, when they are punished; so it is *ghislin*, on the pattern *fi'lin*, from *al-ghasl* (washing). 

The second issue: *Ta'am* (food) is that which is prepared for eating. When the discharge is prepared for the people of the Fire to eat, it becomes food for them. It is also permissible that the meaning is that this was set in place of food, and so it was called food, as the poet said:

*Their greeting among them is a painful striking.*

The greeting is not a striking, but since it was put in its place, it is permissible to call it by that name.

Then the Exalted mentioned who eats the *ghislin*, saying: ﴿None eat it except the sinners﴾. *Al-khati'un* are the sinful, the possessors of errors, those who deliberately commit sin, and they are the polytheists. It was also read *al-khatiyun* (replacing the hamza with a ya') and *al-khatun* (dropping it). It is related from Ibn 'Abbas that he criticised this reading and said: "What is *al-khatiyun*? We all *nakhtu* (step). It is only *al-kha'in* (the sinners). What is *al-sabun*? It is only *al-sabi'un*." It is permissible to answer him that what is meant are those who step over the truth into falsehood and transgress the limits of God.

Know that when the Exalted established the proof for the possibility of the Resurrection, then for its occurrence, then mentioned the states of the blessed and the states of the wretched, He concluded the discourse by exalting the Qur'an, saying:

﴿So I swear by what you see﴾ ﴿and what you do not see﴾. On this there are two issues.

The first issue: Some said: the meaning is "I swear," and *la* is superfluous, or the rejection of a previous statement has preceded it. Others said: *la* here negates the oath, as if He said: "I do not swear," [because] this Qur'an is ﴿the word of a noble messenger﴾, meaning that because of its clarity it does not need an oath. The full treatment of this issue we will mention at the beginning of the surah ﴿I swear by the Day of Resurrection﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 1].

The second issue: His statement ﴿by what you see﴾ and ﴿what you do not see﴾ encompasses all things comprehensively, because they do not go outside two categories: that which sees and that which does not see. So it includes the Creator and the created, this world and the Hereafter, bodies and spirits, humans and jinn, and the apparent and hidden blessings.

Then the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger﴾.

Know that the Exalted mentioned a similar statement in the surah ﴿When the sun is wound up﴾ [al-Takwir: 1]. Most commentators there hold that what is meant is Gabriel, peace be upon him, and most here hold that what is meant is Muhammad ﷺ. As for in the surah ﴿When the sun is wound up﴾, when He said ﴿Indeed, it is the word of a noble messenger﴾ and then said after it ﴿and it is not the word of an accursed devil﴾ [al-Takwir: 25], the meaning was: it is the word of a noble angel, not the word of an accursed devil. So it is correct that what is meant by the noble messenger here is Muhammad ﷺ, and in that surah it is Gabriel, peace be upon him.

At this point the question arises: the Community is in agreement that the Qur'an is the speech of God the Exalted, and then it follows that one single speech is the speech of God the Exalted, and of Gabriel, and of Muhammad, and this is unintelligible. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿A revelation from the Lord of the worlds.﴾

Abu al-Sammal recited ﴿tanzilan﴾ (as a verbal noun), meaning: it was revealed as a revelation.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And if he had fabricated against Us some sayings﴾. It is recited as ﴿wa-law tuquwwila﴾ in the passive voice. Taqawwul (fabricating speech) is the reflexive form (iftial) of qawl (speech), because it involves effort on the part of the one who fabricates. He called the reported sayings "aqawil" (sayings) in order to belittle them, like your saying "al-a'ajib" (the marvels) and "al-adahik" (the jokes); it is as if it were the plural of uf'ulah from qawl. The meaning is: if he had attributed to Us a saying that We had not spoken.

* * *

Then Allah the Exalted says: ﴿We would have seized him by the right hand. Then We would have cut off his aorta﴾. On this there are two issues.

The first issue: concerning the verse, there are several explanations.

The first: its meaning is, "We would have taken hold of his hand, and then We would have struck his neck." He mentioned this as an illustration of what kings do to one who lies against them, for they do not give him respite, but strike his neck at once. He specified the right hand because a killer who wants to strike the back of the neck takes hold with his left hand, and when he wants to strike the neck and bring him down with the sword, which is more severe for the one struck, he takes hold with his right hand because of his looking at the sword. Its meaning is: "We would have seized his right hand." Likewise His saying ﴿We would have cut off his aorta﴾ means "We would have cut off his aorta." This is a clear explanation, and it is related from al-Hasan al-Basri.

The second explanation: al-yamin (the right hand) here means power and ability. This is the view of al-Farra', al-Mubarrad and al-Zajjaj, and they cited the verse of al-Shammakh:

*When a banner is raised for glory,*
*'Arabah meets it with the right hand (yamin).*

The meaning is: "He would have taken away the yamin from him," that is, We would have stripped him of power. The letter ba' (in bil-yamin) on this reading is an extra connective particle. Ibn Qutaybah said: the right hand has taken the place of power, because the strength of everything lies in its right side.

The third explanation: Muqatil said: ﴿We would have seized him by the right hand﴾ [as-Saffat, 28] means "We would have taken vengeance upon him with the truth," and al-yamin in this view means "the truth," as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, you used to come to us from the right side﴾ [as-Saffat, 28], that is, "from the direction of the truth."
